claims: CTE is a progressive, degenerative brain disease.
CTE is caused by repeated head impacts.
CTE is commonly found in contact sport athletes.
CTE is commonly found in military veterans.
CTE is commonly found in those with repetitive brain trauma.
Symptoms of CTE include cognitive decline.
Symptoms of CTE include behavioral changes like aggression.
Symptoms of CTE usually appear years after injury.
CTE can only be definitively diagnosed via autopsy currently.
Symptoms of CTE often emerge 8–10 years after repetitive mild traumatic brain injuries.
Symptoms of CTE tend to follow a progressive, two-stage pattern.
Early symptoms of CTE include impulse control problems.
Early symptoms of CTE include aggression.
Early symptoms of CTE include irritability.
Early symptoms of CTE include anger.
Early symptoms of CTE include depression.
Early symptoms of CTE include paranoia.
Late symptoms of CTE include memory loss.
Late symptoms of CTE include confusion.
Late symptoms of CTE include impaired judgment.
Late symptoms of CTE include dementia.
Symptoms of CTE include headaches.
Symptoms of CTE include dizziness.
Symptoms of CTE include suicidal behavior.
The primary cause of CTE is repeated hits to the head.
Repeated hits to the head include concussions.
Repeated hits to the head include sub-concussive blows that do not cause immediate symptoms.
Repeated head impacts cause tau protein to build up.
Tau buildup forms clumps.
Tau clumps slowly spread through the brain.
Tau clumps kill brain cells.
CTE is frequently found in football athletes.
CTE is frequently found in hockey athletes.
CTE is frequently found in boxing athletes.
CTE is frequently found in rugby athletes.
CTE is frequently found in soccer athletes.
The number of years playing contact sports increases CTE risk.
An earlier age of first exposure increases CTE risk.
Researchers generally categorize CTE progression into four stages.
CTE Stage I includes headaches.
CTE Stage I includes loss of concentration.
CTE Stage I has tau deposits (neurofibrillary tangles - NFTs) in the brain's sulcal depths.
CTE Stage II includes mood swings.
CTE Stage II includes short-term memory loss.
CTE Stage III includes cognitive impairment.
CTE Stage III includes executive dysfunction.
CTE Stage III has widespread tau deposits, including the hippocampus.
CTE Stage IV includes severe, profound memory loss.
CTE Stage IV includes dementia.
CTE Stage IV has significant brain atrophy.
There is no known cure for CTE.
CTE is progressive.
CTE generally gets worse over time.
Treatments for CTE focus on managing symptoms through cognitive therapy.
Treatments for CTE focus on managing symptoms through physical therapy.
Treatments for CTE focus on managing symptoms through occupational therapy.
CTE can lead to permanent loss of memory.
CTE can lead to personality changes.
CTE can lead to loss of independence.
CTE can lead to increased risk of suicide.
CTE cannot be definitively diagnosed in living individuals currently.
Definitive diagnosis of CTE requires microscopic examination of brain tissue after death.
Researchers are actively working on biomarkers for living diagnosis of CTE.
